profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a regional health innovation collaborative evaluating a draft implementation blueprint for adapting the MH ECO theoretical model into a 12-week redesign program across two outpatient mental health clinics and one general medicine service line. The proposal includes peer-facilitated storytelling sessions, staff-patient co-design workshops, a mechanism-tracking template based on the eight proposed change mechanisms, and an internal evaluation plan. The agenda is to review whether the blueprint is ready for pilot approval, identify gaps in facilitation design and evaluation readiness, and decide what revisions are needed before the packet goes to the steering committee. The expected outcome is a conditional approval to proceed with minor revisions, while aligning on what must be updated in the design pack this week.

members.name: Dr. Lena Ortiz
members.expertise: healthcare improvement design, implementation planning, cross-service redesign in hospital and community settings
members.background: Lena is an improvement specialist who has led several patient-experience redesign projects in integrated care systems and now oversees translational design work that turns conceptual models into pilot-ready operational plans.
members.private_state: She wants the blueprint to clear design review today so the pilot keeps its funding timeline, and she is mainly concerned that the proposal looks implementable and governable across multiple services without triggering another round of committee edits.
hidden_assumptions: If a participatory design is 'ready for pilot,' it means the facilitation flow, governance steps, and staffing model are stable enough to run, even if some measurement instruments are refined during the first cycle.
The review's scope is the operational blueprint for workshop delivery and local service adaptation, not a full re-justification of the theoretical model or publication-grade evaluation design.
When the blueprint says 'peer facilitation,' it naturally includes trained lived-experience workers already embedded in the clinics, with external coaching only as backup.
The 'first cycle' of the pilot refers to the initial 12-week implementation wave at each participating service, using whatever local cadence fits that service.

members.name: Prof. Marcus Ng
members.expertise: co-design theory, realist and process evaluation, qualitative mechanism mapping in health services research
members.background: Marcus is an academic partner brought in to ensure the MH ECO adaptation preserves the underlying theory of change and yields interpretable evidence about mechanisms across settings.
members.private_state: He wants the blueprint to preserve theoretical fidelity and produce data strong enough for cross-site learning, and he is concerned that operational shortcuts will make the pilot uninterpretable even if it launches on time.
hidden_assumptions: If a participatory design is 'ready for pilot,' it means the mechanism definitions, observation protocol, and cross-site evaluation logic are sufficiently specified before any sessions begin.
The review implicitly includes whether the blueprint remains faithful to MH ECO as an explanatory model, because implementation details cannot be separated from theory in this kind of design.
When the blueprint says 'peer facilitation,' it implies facilitators who are independent of the service hierarchy so participants can speak without institutional pressure.
The 'first cycle' refers to the first common round of workshops conducted under the standardized research protocol across all sites, enabling comparison.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the blueprint is 'ready for pilot' after a few refinements.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready for pilot' means the program can be launched with a stable facilitation plan, staffing assignments, and governance approvals, while some evaluation details can be finalized during early implementation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready for pilot' means the mechanism coding framework, observation template, and cross-site evidence strategy are specified enough in advance that the pilot can generate interpretable findings from day one.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In a design review, 'ready' is a routine approval phrase that sounds shared and competent; both expect some minor edits afterward, so the difference in threshold remains hidden beneath polite agreement.

misalignment_points.topic: Who counts as a peer facilitator
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both endorse keeping 'peer facilitation' at the center of the design.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means experienced lived-experience staff already employed within the participating clinics, because they are easiest to schedule, orient, and integrate into the redesign workflow.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means facilitators with lived experience who are structurally independent from the clinic being reviewed, so their role preserves participant candor and the empowerment logic of MH ECO.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'peer facilitation' is strongly positive and domain-familiar, so each assumes the other shares the standard meaning they use in their own professional circles; neither sees a need to unpack employment relationship or institutional independence.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the design review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the blueprint' and discuss tightening it before sending the packet forward.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the blueprint as the workshop sequence, staffing, consent pathway, and implementation materials that the steering committee needs for operational approval.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the blueprint as including the mechanism map, relational transition definitions, and analytic plan because those are integral to whether the model has been faithfully translated.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are literally looking at the same document set and use the same noun, but the packet combines operational appendices and theory/evaluation sections, allowing each to assume their own boundary of what is under review.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'first cycle' they are talking about
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that some elements can be refined after 'the first cycle.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the first 12-week local implementation wave at each service, which may start at different dates and adapt to local scheduling realities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the first synchronized round of workshops across all three sites under the common protocol, after which cross-site comparison would be reviewed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The project plan uses the phrase 'first cycle' repeatedly without pinning it to a single calendar object; because both expect iteration, the phrase seems harmlessly shared rather than indexically ambiguous.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get this through design review today so the steering committee packet can go out on time and we don't reopen the whole thing. For me, the blueprint is the operational pack: workshop flow, staffing, consent route, escalation steps, and local adaptation notes. If that is stable, it's ready for pilot. We do not need to settle every evaluation detail before launch.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. What I'd like us to do today is confirm whether the MH ECO adaptation blueprint is ready for pilot, note any final tightening needed, and get the packet into shape for steering committee circulation this week.

turns.inner_thought: The design is promising, but I need to make sure the blueprint preserves the theory of change well enough that the pilot yields interpretable cross-site learning. To me the blueprint absolutely includes the mechanism map, relational transition definitions, and evaluation logic. If those are underspecified, it is not really ready for pilot no matter how polished the operations look.
turns.utterance: Yes, overall it's in a strong place. My main interest is making sure the blueprint holds the mechanism logic clearly enough that the pilot can actually teach us something across sites, not just get underway.

turns.inner_thought: The practical core is sound: storytelling sessions, then co-design workshops, with the service teams and lived-experience staff already identified. Peer facilitation should stay central, and in my mind that means the trained lived-experience workers embedded in each clinic, because they're available, trusted locally, and can be scheduled without creating another layer of contracting.
turns.utterance: From an implementation point of view, the flow is now fairly clean: the storytelling sessions lead into the co-design workshops, and the staffing model is workable at each site. I do think we should keep peer facilitation at the center of the design, because that's what gives the sessions their credibility and continuity.

turns.inner_thought: I agree completely on peer facilitation, but only if it functions as genuine peer facilitation in the MH ECO sense. I am assuming facilitators will have enough independence from the local service hierarchy that participants can speak candidly without feeling watched by the organization being discussed. If that distance is protected, the trust mechanism has a chance to operate.
turns.utterance: I agree with that completely. Keeping peer facilitation central is essential, and it will do a lot for trust and openness if the facilitators hold enough distance from the local service context.

turns.inner_thought: What remains before committee is mainly housekeeping: tighten the consent wording, sharpen the session guide, make the governance path read clearly. I do not want us delaying approval because the internal evaluation appendix isn't publication-ready. We can tune instruments during the first 12-week wave at each service once we see what works locally.
turns.utterance: As I see it, the main remaining edits are really around tightening the consent language and making the session guide a little crisper. Some of the evaluation detail can be tuned after the first cycle without holding up launch.

turns.inner_thought: Iteration after the first synchronized round is fine, but only if we begin with stable mechanism definitions, observation prompts, and a shared evaluation frame across all sites. Otherwise the first cycle won't generate comparable evidence and we'll lose the chance to understand what is happening. I need to secure enough specification before any sessions start.
turns.utterance: I think refining after the first cycle makes sense, but only if the mechanism definitions and observation prompts are stable before that cycle begins. Otherwise we'll struggle to interpret what we're seeing.

turns.inner_thought: He's asking for clarity, which is fine, but I need to keep this centered on what the committee is actually approving. The blueprint they care about is whether the workshops can run safely and consistently across services: logistics, escalation pathways, staffing, adaptation boundaries. I don't want this meeting to slide into a full theory defense.
turns.utterance: That's fair. I suppose the question for today is whether the blueprint itself is complete enough for committee review. From my side, I want to be sure the workshop logistics, escalation pathways, and local adaptation notes are all tight before we send the packet forward.

turns.inner_thought: For me, the blueprint is not complete unless the mechanism language is sharper. Reviewers need to see how recognition, dialogue, and enactment are being translated into something traceable; otherwise the adaptation risks becoming a generic workshop series. I can ask for wording changes without opening a larger argument.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think the blueprint would also benefit from slightly clearer wording around recognition, dialogue, and enactment, so reviewers can see how the relational transitions will actually be traced through the work.

turns.inner_thought: I can accommodate that with a light revision, but I do not want to destabilize the facilitator plan. The current roster is already lined up through the clinics, and changing it now would create delay. A short debrief template after each session should be enough structure to reassure Marcus without reopening staffing.
turns.utterance: That sounds manageable. My preference would be a light-touch revision: keep the current facilitator roster, add a short debrief template for peers after each session, and make the wording changes where they strengthen the read for committee.

turns.inner_thought: A debrief template is useful, and if the peer facilitators are properly oriented in the common protocol before the first synchronized round, that should support consistency. I'm still assuming those peers will be positioned with enough independence for the model to function as intended. I don't need to press the point if the protocol language can carry it.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think the debrief idea would help. It should work well once the peer facilitators are oriented in the common protocol before the first cycle starts.

turns.inner_thought: Good, that sounds like agreement. If I make a few wording edits and add the debrief piece, we should be able to present this as ready for pilot tomorrow. The committee mainly needs to see a governable, implementable design; I can keep any unresolved measurement refinements moving within early implementation.
turns.utterance: Alright, then my takeaway is that with some minor wording changes the design looks ready for pilot. I'll revise the packet today and aim to circulate to committee tomorrow.

turns.inner_thought: It's close, provided the updated blueprint tightens the mechanism language enough that the pilot begins on a theoretically coherent footing. I want one more look before it goes forward, just to protect fidelity and the chances of usable cross-site evidence. It sounds as though we're aligned.
turns.utterance: That works for me. It's very close, and I'd just appreciate a quick look at the updated blueprint once that mechanism language is tightened, so the pilot can proceed cleanly.
